item.title: Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2 (222 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://pwn.ai/blog/firecracker-escape, See on Hacker News

Firecracker is supposed to keep untrusted code inside a microVM. We escaped it and achieved code execution as root on the host.

We found how it saved registers, changed where it would resume, and made it execute a call of our choosing when it returned from KVM. The guest then restored the temporary stack changes. Firecracker kept running, and the VM remained accessible over SSH.

PwnEscape Part 1 introduced the host memory primitive behind this work. Here we follow the next part of the chain: using that access to find Firecracker in memory and take over a live thread from inside the guest. This is a continuation to show CVE-2026-99999 on a Firecracker setup.

00 / Choosing where to take control

A Firecracker microVM has a process on the host that manages it. Each virtual CPU, or vCPU, has a thread in that process. The thread enters KVM to run the guest and returns to Firecracker when an event needs handling in userspace. Firecracker documents this arrangement in its architecture overview.

The call that runs the virtual CPU looks like this:

While the thread is in that system call, the host kernel holds its saved userspace registers in a structure called pt_regs. These registers describe the Firecracker thread: its instruction pointer says where execution should resume, and its stack pointer says which userspace stack it should use.

That made the return from KVM_RUN an attractive target. If we could locate and modify the saved frame, we could choose the code Firecracker executed when the thread returned to userspace. A guest operation that caused such a return would provide the trigger.

We already had access to selected host physical memory through a guest mapping. To use it, we needed to identify the Firecracker process, find code we could call in that process, and locate the register frame belonging to its active vCPU thread. The starting point was a page of memory we controlled inside the guest.

Figure 1. The guest identifies its Firecracker process, finds the saved registers for a vCPU thread, and redirects the thread when it returns from KVM.

01 / Finding our guest page on the host

The guest and host use different physical address spaces. A page has a guest physical address, or GPA, inside the VM and a host physical address, or HPA, in the machine backing it. On the target, Extended Page Tables (EPT) provide the translation between them.

We placed a recognizable byte pattern, a nonce, in a guest page. The first resolver took that page's known GPA and its contents as inputs. Together, they gave us an address to translate and a way to check whether the translation reached our page.

The resolver searched the host physical ranges covered by the memory primitive for candidate EPT roots. An EPT root is the starting point of the translation tables. For each candidate, the resolver followed the entries selected by the guest address until it reached a physical page, then checked that page for the nonce.

The snippets below are explanatory pseudocode with descriptive helper names. They show the data passed between stages and the checks used to connect them.

The nonce check connected a proposed translation to memory we controlled. The broader search produced two candidates; validation of the nested page tables reduced them to one EPT root. Walking that root gave us the host physical address of our guest page.

We called this result guest_page_hpa and passed it to the next resolver. We now had a recognizable object in host memory. The next task was finding the host process that mapped it.

02 / Finding the Firecracker process

Firecracker maps memory used by the guest into its own address space. That mapping gave us a way to work backward from the guest page to the process.

Host processes use page tables to translate their virtual addresses into physical memory. The top level is called the page global directory, or PGD. Recovering the appropriate PGD would let us translate addresses inside Firecracker and read its code and stack through the memory primitive.

Our reverse mapper searched the native host page tables for a mapping of guest_page_hpa. A normal page table walk starts with a virtual address and produces a physical address. Here, we looked for a mapping to a physical page we already knew, then recovered the virtual address and page table root associated with it.

The check runs in both directions:

This connected the host process's virtual mapping to the physical page found through EPT. The reverse mapper returned one validated address space. We retained its root as host_pgd and used it to inspect the process.

The next resolver looked for the Firecracker executable in those mappings. It identified an ELF image and checked a known byte sequence in Firecracker's write(2) wrapper. That connected the recovered address space to the binary we were targeting.

ASLR changes where an executable is loaded. The difference between an address in the ELF image and its corresponding runtime address is the load bias. Once the mapper had identified the image, it could recover that bias and use it to locate the code required by the exploit:

The mapper returned the load bias as firecracker_base. With that value and host_pgd, we could locate code in the running process, translate its virtual address to host physical memory, and compare the bytes there with the expected binary.

We checked three locations: the write(2) wrapper that would produce our proof, the continuation after the KVM ioctl, and a short xor eax,eax; ret sequence needed to return cleanly. Their purposes become relevant when we construct the return path below.

At this point, the guest could inspect the Firecracker image and its private mappings. We still needed the saved registers of the thread currently running our VM.

Figure 2. The nonce identifies the guest page in host memory. Its mapping leads to a host page table root, which lets the next resolver locate and validate the Firecracker image.

03 / Locating the live vCPU frame

The frame finder took host_pgd and firecracker_base from the preceding stages. It used them to recognize the host thread's saved state.

The most useful clue was the return address. A vCPU thread in KVM_RUN should have a saved instruction pointer at the corresponding ioctl continuation in Firecracker. We could calculate that address from the validated binary and its load bias.

We then searched host memory for a pt_regs frame consistent with that call. An address match alone would also pick up stale stack contents, so the candidate had to satisfy several related checks:

Saved stateWhat we checked
System callThe syscall identity and in-progress state matched an active ioctl.
Request argumentThe ioctl request was KVM_RUN.
File descriptorThe descriptor fell within the helper's expected range.
Instruction pointerIt matched the validated Firecracker ioctl continuation.
Stack pointerIt translated through the recovered host PGD.
Segment selectors and flagsThey described a valid return to userspace.
Caller return addressIt fell inside the validated Firecracker text mapping.

The stack check tied the frame to the same address space we had recovered from the guest page. The instruction and caller addresses tied it to the Firecracker image. The syscall fields tied it to the operation running the vCPU.

The search left one candidate. Its location was stored as frame_hpa, the host physical address of the saved register frame. We passed it, the PGD, and the load bias to the final helper.

Before changing memory, the helper repeated the code signature, frame, and stack checks. This ensured that the active stage used the same process state the resolvers had identified. The subsequent execution and recovery checks would establish that the selected frame was live.

Figure 3. The candidate register frame must agree with the KVM ioctl, the recovered process page tables, and the validated Firecracker code.

04 / Redirecting the return from KVM

We chose a simple payload: make the Firecracker process write a recognizable string to its own stderr. This would give the host runner an observable result from the process we had taken over.

The string was N8V23M2\n, seven characters followed by a newline. It occupies eight bytes and fits in one stack word. The call we wanted Firecracker to execute was:

Here 2 is Firecracker's stderr file descriptor. The buffer pointer must refer to the string in Firecracker's address space, so we stored the string on its private userspace stack.

We saved three stack words before modifying them. One held the string; the other two held the return addresses for the temporary call sequence. We then changed the saved register frame to supply the wrapper address, its arguments, and a stack pointer for that sequence:

Returning from write also needed care. A successful write of eight bytes returns 8, while a successful KVM_RUN call returns zero. We placed the address of xor eax,eax; ret first in the return sequence. It clears the return value before the second address brings execution back to Firecracker's original ioctl continuation.

The resulting control flow was:

With the stack and saved registers prepared, the guest wrote one byte to its serial port. That operation caused the vCPU thread to return from KVM_RUN. The kernel restored the modified registers, and Firecracker entered the write wrapper with our arguments.

The wrapper emitted the marker, the return sequence cleared eax, and the thread rejoined its original execution path. After control returned to the guest, the helper restored all three stack words.

Figure 4. The saved register frame enters the write wrapper. Two return addresses lead through the return-value adjustment and back into the original Firecracker path.

05 / Checking execution and recovery

The host runner captured Firecracker's stderr separately from the guest. The complete output was:

The capture contained exactly eight bytes, including the final newline. Firecracker was still running, guest SSH was responsive, and the helper had restored the three temporary stack words.

We checked recovery with a fresh pass that made no memory changes. It was given the same frame address and repeated the register, code, and stack checks after the trigger. The checks passed, and it found no stale marker in the temporary stack location.

These observations answered three different questions. The guest log recorded the trigger and restoration. The host capture showed that Firecracker executed the selected operation. The final validation checked the state after execution.

CheckRecorded result
Firecracker stderrOne copy of the marker, eight bytes in total
Firecracker processPID 2936, alive after the trigger
Guest healthSSH responsive; uptime 1615.72 seconds
Temporary stack stateAll three original words restored
Executable text and shared librariesUnmodified
Host kernel errors after the triggerNone observed
Validation after restorationThe supplied frame address and surrounding invariants passed

Figure 5. The guest log, Firecracker stderr capture, and final validation record the trigger, host execution, and restored state.

06 / Root execution on the host

By the time the marker appeared, the guest had selected the host thread's instruction pointer, function arguments, stack data, and return path. Firecracker executed the call using its own privileges.

The target was Firecracker v1.16.1 on x86-64, with host kernel 7.0.0-1011-aws and guest kernel 6.18.44+. We launched Firecracker directly as root under systemd-run and pinned it with taskset. Consequently, the controlled call executed as root on the host.

The existing write wrapper gave us a compact proof of that control. Extending it to other calls would require choosing code and arguments compatible with the process's mappings and syscall policy.

The configuration used here had no jailer. Firecracker's production containment includes dropping privileges and restricting the process through namespaces and seccomp. A deployment using those controls requires a separate assessment of the privileges and resources available after compromising its VMM.

The address discovery is what lets the exploit follow the running instance. The EPT resolver connects a guest page to host memory; the reverse mapper recovers the host address space; the image mapper locates Firecracker under ASLR; and the frame finder identifies the vCPU's saved state. Adapting the final stage to another build requires validating that binary's code signatures and return path.

The guest had used access to host memory to take over the thread running the VM itself. A serial write supplied the trigger, and the next userspace operation belonged to us.

Captured resolver values and artifacts

The following values come from the preserved execution record. The methods above use symbolic names so that the role of each value is clear; this table connects those names to the recorded addresses.

ValueRecorded addressWhere it enters the chain
guest_gpa0x08f03000The guest physical address of the nonce page, supplied to the first resolver
guest_page_hpa0x165610000The host address of that page, found by the EPT resolver
host_pgd0x14afc2000The host page table root recovered by the reverse mapper
firecracker_base0x7298c2400000The Firecracker load bias recovered by the image mapper
frame_hpa0x13a5bff48The saved register frame selected for the active stage

The records use run ID eventpath-v23-0907self02 and boot ID 2b3cd5ac-2311-427f-a50a-6a79ecb8daa7. These identifiers connect the resolver records, host capture, and validation after restoration.

The earlier memory provider also received host-selected task and canary page frame numbers as independent validation overlays after constructing the memory aperture. Those addresses were not consumed by the EPT resolver, reverse mapper, Firecracker mapper, frame finder, or final marker helper.

The release bundle contains the final helper source, JSONL resolver records, host capture, recovery manifest, four preserved read-only resolver binaries with provenance, and SHA-256 manifests. The final helper accepts the PGD, load bias, and frame HPA produced by the resolvers. Its checks cover the run identifier, address ranges, code signatures, saved registers, and stack geometry; its dry-run mode performs validation without writing memory.

shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS

item.title: GitHub's new Git storage architecture (130 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/inside-githubs-new-git-storage-architecture/, See on Hacker News

Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running.

Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post, we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage.

We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.

The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components.

Building for agent scale

We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes:

  1. Horizontal scale is how many developers and agents can work across many repositories. Many of GitHub’s current approaches on this axis have been battle-tested over the years and are carried forward to the new architecture: partitioning of tenants across infrastructure, isolation and/or fairness enforcement of tenant traffic, and load-aware routing, to name a few.
  2. Vertical scale is how many developers and agents can work on one repository. As agents write more code, we expect individual repositories to get larger and busier, so most of our requirements came from the vertical axis.

Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes.

We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then.

We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to:

  • Accept thousands of writes per second.
  • Support multiple writer nodes. There are two reasons for this:
    • Experience has taught us that indexing incoming packs and checking object connectivity are the most CPU-expensive parts of a write, and that cost scales with the size of the write, so a single node will become compute-bound quickly.
    • Spreading that work across many nodes improves fault tolerance and shortens recovery when a node fails.
  • Minimize commit latency. An agent waits on each push before it moves to its next step.
  • Record changes in order for each reference with the ability to quickly linearize across references. A virtual replica that falls behind needs to catch up by downloading only the data it needs to serve the incoming request.
  • Keep reads cheap when nothing has changed, which is the common case given the read-to-write ratio.
  • Let each component scale independently.

On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally.

Introducing “Project Rubicon”

In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We’ll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it “Rubicon,” a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development.

Let’s walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new.

Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica’s local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.

Spokes routes a repository’s traffic to the same virtual replicas when it can, which keeps their caches warm and latency low, but nothing about correctness depends on a request landing on any particular virtual replica. When a virtual replica goes away, the repository’s other virtual replicas keep serving, and a replacement fills its cache as traffic arrives.

When a repository gets busy, we add more virtual replicas. Separately, a fleet of compaction nodes works in the background, directly against Blob Storage and Ref-CAS, to merge each repository’s packs and remove unreachable objects. That work never runs on a virtual replica, meaning their CPU and memory can be almost entirely dedicated to serving requests.

Durable state lives in two places:

  1. Git objects, in the form of packs and auxiliary read acceleration data, live in Azure Blob Storage.
  2. References and the list of packs that make up the repository (the pack manifest) live in a separate replicated log service we call Ref-CAS (for “Reference Compare-and-Swap”).

Let’s walk the architecture from the perspective of a write and a read:

  • Write: a virtual replica indexes the incoming pack and uploads it to Blob Storage, then commits one transaction to Ref-CAS that lists the pack in the manifest and updates the references. Later, a compaction node merges that pack with others to keep reads fast.
  • Read: a virtual replica checks its reference version with Ref-CAS, pulls the packs it needs from Blob Storage into its cache, and serves the read from there.

There are many distinct approaches we’ve taken within the new architecture, from the software stack on the virtual replicas to how traffic routing and workload scheduling are tuned for different use cases (e.g., many small repos vs. one large one). Let’s dive deep into two components of the architecture and tell their stories centered on the two design principles.

Minimizing coordination: mutating reference state at high throughput

Object storage services like Azure Blob Storage are incredibly good at what they do, and natural fits for many data-heavy applications like source code storage. They are durable and replicated, hold as much as we need them to, have a relatively low cost per byte, and deliver exceptionally high aggregate throughput so long as traffic is spread across many keys. As a result, nearly everything durable in the new Git storage architecture lives in Azure Blob Storage, including:

  • Packs and indexes written by pushes, compaction, and garbage collection.
  • Various read accelerators (like multi-pack indexes, reachability bitmaps, and some custom formats) that our maintenance process builds from those packs.
  • Records that let compaction and garbage collection resume or audit their work, along with the leases that compaction nodes use to claim work.
  • Cached responses for frequently repeated fetches.
  • Checkpoints for the reference state of the repository, though not the authoritative state used to serve requests.

Most of that data is written once to a distinct key and never changes afterward, which is what makes it highly suitable for Blob Storage.

References are the opposite. A busy repository’s references are a relatively small piece of state that many writes race to update at the same time. That access pattern is harder to serve from Blob Storage, and our first prototypes showed us why. Object storage for this kind of workload is an intuitive choice, and one that works well up to a certain level of scale: conditional writes give a compare-and-swap for free, and the data is already durable and replicated. However, we ran into a difficult set of choices, illustrated below by two approaches we tried.

Our first approach was a write-ahead log for all of a repository’s references, indexed by a single blob. Every update is a conditional write against that blob. It’s correct, and reads are cheap: a virtual replica asks whether the blob has changed, and if it hasn’t, it’s done. Writes are where it falls short. Only one conditional write to a blob can be in flight at a time, so even when we batch every push that arrives during a write into the next one, the repository’s write ceiling is one write per round trip to a single blob. In practice, this netted us write throughput in the mid-hundreds per second.

Our second approach split the references across several segment blobs, with each reference hashing to one of them. Writes to references in different segments no longer wait on each other, which raises the ceiling. But a read now has to check every segment to know whether anything changed, and it’s only as fast as the slowest segment. We’d traded write latency for read latency, and reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. We can visualize this by showing multiple writes and a read side by side:

Neither option met every requirement, so we built something else: a replicated log service dedicated to references, or the Ref-CAS service. This is the (small) consensus group we said at the end of the last post was still somewhere in the stack. Here’s how it works.

Each reference update in Ref-CAS is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum. A transaction locks only the references it touches, checks that each one still has the value the writer expects, and becomes visible once a majority of the log’s replicas have recorded it. Agents mostly push to their own branches, so most updates don’t contend, and they replicate in parallel. When two pushes do update the same reference, only one will append to the log.

Each commit to Ref-CAS gets a log sequence number (LSN), and the repository’s version is the LSN of its latest commit. Reads start with a version check against that version. A virtual replica sends the version of the reference state it already holds. If that version is still current, the reply carries no references at all, and an unchanged repository costs a single comparison. If the virtual replica is behind, it gets back the current references and version, along with pointers to pack data and anything else that needs to be known, such as when the last garbage collection cycle occurred.

Unlike the consensus group in our legacy architecture, Ref-CAS never holds or validates object data. It only stores pointers to it. A virtual replica uploads a push’s pack to Blob Storage before it commits the reference transaction. A reference only ever points at objects that are already durable.

These approaches allow us to transact reference state alone in the tens of thousands of operations per second, and provide a baseline for additional annotations on the replication log that help reads decide what to download for a given request.

But supporting thousands of writes per second on a single repository creates a second-order problem: maintaining the performance of reads and writes. For that, we needed a different approach to compaction.

Decoupling storage from compute: compaction at thousands of writes per second

Every push adds a pack to Blob Storage. Git can serve a repository from many packs, but each additional pack makes lookups slightly more expensive, so the pack count can’t grow without bound. In our legacy architecture, compaction runs on the same replicas that serve traffic, and it has to run on every replica. In the new architecture, it runs entirely in the background on separate nodes, directly against durable storage, using the Ref-CAS service to notify virtual replicas of the evolving state.

Compaction nodes each claim ownership over a subset of the repository’s data via a lease, which allows us to scale compaction horizontally. Here’s how one compaction node works through a single shard of a repository’s packs:

The node first takes a lease on the shard in Blob Storage, so only one node compacts a shard at a time. Meanwhile, virtual replicas keep uploading packs and listing them in the pack manifest. The node reads the manifest to find new packs and collects them into an open segment, which is effectively a holding ground for data about to be compacted. When the segment reaches a defined limit based on pack count, size, or age, it seals the segment so it accepts no new packs, then combines its packs into fewer, larger ones. While compaction happens, the next segment for the shard can begin capturing its input packs. Before anything is published, the node checks that the new packs contain exactly the same objects as the inputs. It then uploads the new packs and adds them to the manifest. A second transaction removes the inputs from the manifest, and cleanup deletes them later.

To scale out, this process runs independently for many shards at once. Each pack’s hash maps to a shard, so adding shards and nodes adds compaction throughput. A compacted pack that’s still under the size limit goes back into a shard by its own hash and merges again, so packs grow in tiers until they reach the limit. The net result is an effectively flat pack count while pushes climb:

Compaction merges packs, but it keeps every object. Garbage collection is the step that removes objects nothing references anymore, like the ones left behind by deleted branches and force-pushes. In our new architecture, garbage collection works very similarly to compaction by using dedicated workers to handle the compute-heavy portion. It also has a few special behaviors for safely removing data, which are worthy of their own discussion.

Using these approaches, we’ve been able to consistently demonstrate a flat latency curve as writes climb, and we have other planned optimizations to make the compaction and garbage collection processes themselves more performant.

What comes next

The two principles we started with let each part of this architecture scale on its own. We scale reads and writes by adding virtual replicas. Ref-CAS orders each reference independently instead of the whole repository. We scale maintenance by adding compaction nodes. Our goal is for every repository, from one developer’s side project to the busiest monorepo, to run on the same architecture with no special handling for the busy ones. Repositories don’t stay small. A side project can pick up a fleet of agents overnight, and it shouldn’t need a migration or special handling from us to keep up. One architecture also means every improvement we make reaches every repository at once.

This foundation lets us do a lot more. We’re focused on three areas next: scaling the architecture beyond what we can predict we’ll need today, making agents more efficient at the work they do on GitHub, and evolving Git itself for agentic development.

Improving the architecture

We have plans to take this architecture further. Each of these improvements lets a repository handle more activity while reducing the work behind each request:

  • Read only what’s needed. Fetch a single object from Blob Storage instead of the whole pack that holds it.
  • Organize packs by type. Group commits, trees, and blobs into their own packs. Many requests then touch less data.
  • Partial replicas. Serve requests without every pack on local disk.
  • Materialized views. Keep repository data in ready-to-use forms, like prepared archives, a near-live shallow copy of the default branch, and agent session context stored alongside each commit.
  • Global replicas. Place replicas in any region, close to the workloads that use them. Reads stay within bounded staleness of the latest write.
  • Scale to zero. Grow and shrink the fleet with the repositories that are actually active.

Efficient agent operations on GitHub

Scaling the infrastructure is one side of supporting agents. The other side is making each agent operation cheaper: fewer bytes to fetch, fewer round trips, and less waiting on changes. Each of these fast-follow items builds on the storage work in this post:

  • Work without a clone. Many agent tasks never need a full working tree. They need a handful of files and enough context to make a change. They can read both straight from the server.
  • Atomic commit API. Land a multi-file change in one operation. The whole change commits, or it’s rejected cleanly on conflict.
  • Event streams. Agents and the systems around them work best with real-time information. A generic event stream lets them subscribe to changes and react as they happen.

Improving Git for agents

We also have work to do in Git itself. GitHub has been a longtime contributor to the Git project, and we’re not stopping now. A few examples of the work we’re excited to continue:

  • Lightweight clones. Partial clone, shallow clone, and sparse checkout each let an agent fetch less. Each one has gaps. They don’t always work well together, either. We want to improve each piece and make them fit.
  • Remove hidden scaling costs. Git still has code paths that slow down much faster than the repository grows. Recent releases fixed several of them, but we expect to find more.
  • Faster history walks. Metadata like the commit-graph can answer merge-base and reachability questions without walking every commit. That matters most when an agent’s API call turns into Git work on the server.
  • Avoid common gotchas. Agents make the same mistakes developers do. Git can catch more of the common ones and warn before they cause damage.

Agents have changed how software gets built. GitHub and Git are changing with it. We’re excited to take this new architecture across the starting line. It’s available in a limited private preview now, with a broader rollout early next year. We can’t wait to see what teams build when the number of agents working on a repository is limited by their ideas. We’ll keep evolving Git and GitHub alongside our customers and the Git community.

Written by

Distinguished Engineer

Brian is a Principal Software Engineer working on the storage and core services that power all repository interactions on GitHub.

When customers order food online, they expect a familiar experience: find their restaurant, choose their meal, and pay. Increasingly, criminals are exploiting that familiarity by creating convincing clones of restaurant ordering websites, right down to the original site's underlying code.

In early November 2026, InfoHawk researchers investigated a collection of suspicious websites that appear to be part of one or more coordinated restaurant impersonation and payment-skimming operations.

Across two research passes, we identified 820 domains impersonating 35 restaurant brands. Of those, 808 use the .delivery top-level domain, and the rest use .com or .shop.

The scale is concerning, but what makes these sites particularly dangerous is how convincing they can be.

These aren't ordinary fake websites

The investigation began with a suspicious domain: mlckessejersstey[.]delivery.

The site impersonated Jersey Mike's, the popular sandwich chain, and reproduced its online ordering experience.

Rather than simply displaying a crude imitation of the restaurant's website, the attackers used a more sophisticated approach: reverse-proxying the legitimate site while replacing the checkout payment form with a malicious one.

A reverse proxy can retrieve content from a legitimate website and present it to visitors under a different domain. This allows an attacker-controlled site to display genuine pages and assets while selectively modifying the parts of the experience that matter to the attacker.

In this case, the malicious checkout requested credit card information and also asked customers for the SMS verification code sent by their bank.

This is a particularly dangerous combination. Capturing a credit card number is valuable to criminals; obtaining a one-time verification code could also help them authorize fraudulent transactions, depending on how the victim's bank uses that code.

For consumers, the experience can appear nearly indistinguishable from ordering directly from the restaurant. The site looks familiar, the menu and ordering flow can behave normally, and the fraudulent payment form appears at the moment a customer expects to pay.

Importantly, this does not require the legitimate restaurant's website to have been hacked. The attackers can operate on infrastructure they control while using the authentic restaurant website as the source of the content they display.

Impersonated brands

Mostly .delivery typosquats, plus a few look-alike .com and .shop names, found across two research passes. "Seen" is the range of registration or scan dates we have for a brand's domains, all in 2026. Open a brand to see its domains.

How the attack works

Each clone is a reverse proxy: a server that sits between the victim and the real restaurant site, fetches every page from the real site as it is requested, edits it on the way through, and passes it on. Menus, prices, store hours, and the cart are live and correct, because they come from the real site. Only the payment step is replaced. Described from mlckessejersstey[.]delivery (Jersey Mike's); we believe the clones of the other brands run the same kit.

  1. The victim arrives from a search ad

    A Google Search ad imitates the restaurant's listing and shows a look-alike domain. The domain is behind Cloudflare, so its real server is hidden, and Cloudflare gives it a valid certificate automatically (Google Trust Services here), so the browser shows "Connection is secure".

  2. Every page is fetched live from the real site

    The proxy forwards each request to the restaurant's own servers, adjusting the host name and cookies, and relays the answer. The real site's headers come through (on Jersey Mike's, x-powered-by: Nuxt and Amazon CloudFront headers), which is how we could tell which paths came from the real site and which from the scammer's server.

  3. Addresses are rewritten to keep the victim on the fake domain

    The proxy replaces the brand's own host names in pages, scripts, and redirects with the fake domain, and maps each backend to a path on it, such as /__bapi__/ or /__payments__/. Store lookup, menus, login, and cart all work, because those calls go back through the proxy to the real APIs. Even the brand's own bot-detection script still runs, with its endpoints rewritten.

  4. Three scripts are injected into every page

    A script blocker patches HTMLScriptElement.prototype.src so that listed scripts never load (on Jersey Mike's, the OneTrust cookie banner and Branch, which could send phone users to the app or the real domain). _jmu() finds the real checkout payment frame and points it at /js/index.html on the fake domain; a MutationObserver puts the fake one back whenever the page restores the real one. _chkT() reads the order total from the "Place order" button every half second and saves it, so the fake form shows the right amount.

  5. The card form is the scammer's

    A few paths are answered by the scammer's server instead of the real site: /js/* (the card form and its scripts) and /payment/socket.io. The form looks like part of checkout. On submit it collects every field (card number, expiry, CVV, name, phone) and sends it, with the site name, to the operator over a live socket.io connection.

  6. An operator gets past the bank's check live

    We believe a person watching a control panel uses the card elsewhere and, when the bank challenges that payment, tells the victim's page what to show next: "card declined, try another", a page asking for the SMS code (/js/confirmation/), an "approve in your bank app" page (/js/app/), or "invalid code, try again". We believe the code the victim types is what lets the operator's charge through 3-D Secure.

  7. The victim is sent away

    When the operator marks it a success, the page sets a cookie valid=77777 lasting until 2038 and sends the victim to another chain's real site (href.li/?https://www.jimmyjohns.com/; href.li hides where they came from). No order reaches the restaurant: the real payment step never runs, so there is no confirmation email and no food. We believe the victim's card is then charged for whatever the operator bought.

Why this design. The clone never goes out of date, the victim builds a real order with a real total before anything looks wrong, and one kit works against any restaurant by changing the target site, the domain, and a few path rules. The scammer's server does very little work, which makes it cheap to move. Some variants skip the payment wording and only pin the frame's address, re-setting it every time the page changes it.

Distribution of the Delivery Scam

Searching Google's ad archive (Ads Transparency Center) for the domains in our first sweep found at least 47 Google Search text ads between July 7, 2026, and October 20, 2026, run under at least 46 separate advertiser accounts with at least 43 different, unrelated-looking business names (construction firms, a reptile rescue, a watch company). The ads below are a sub-sample: we searched only for the domains in our first sweep, so there are likely more. Each ad imitates a restaurant's search listing and shows a look-alike domain. Most ran for 1–4 days, usually starting days after the domain was registered.

Status: On November 4, 2026, 367 of the 820 domains still served a site, so they could be getting traffic through means other than ads. None of the ads below were still running on November 3, 2026, but this scam may also be running through other ads, or other means. Google's public Ads Transparency pages now show "Can't find ad" for the creatives and "No ads found" for the domains we checked, which suggests Google has taken them down; the "Ads Transparency page" links below will likely not load. The images and text here come from InfoHawk's own capture of Google's archive, made on or before November 3, 2026. Of the 47 ads below, 41 have Google's rendered image; the rest show the text from Google's ad preview. Domains in the image ads were read from the image and may contain small reading errors.

Jimmy John's20Jul 7 – Sep 18
Firehouse Subs12Jul 28 – Sep 30
Dave's Hot Chicken11Aug 18 – Oct 20
Jersey Mike's4Jul 21 – Jul 31

Hosting

Most of the clones sit behind Cloudflare (AS13335), which hides the real servers: 761 of the 820 domains use Cloudflare nameservers, 11 use other nameservers, and 48 have none. Another cluster of 68 domains is tied to an Amazon Web Services (AWS) server. Some of its sites are served straight from that server, in Frankfurt (3.79.192.101) through my-ndns.com nameservers, and its pages carry a different injected script (/static/<name>-fix.js). It uses the same cloning technique, but we found nothing that shows the same people run it, so these sites may come from more than one operator using the same kit.

In our first sweep of 255 domains, 251 were registered at Dynadot, spread across 111 Cloudflare nameserver pairs.

What this means for restaurant brands

These clones don't need to break into a restaurant's systems. They borrow the real site, page by page, and insert the attack only at the moment a customer pays. That makes them hard to spot from the outside, but it also means the brand's own servers see every page the clone serves. Brands and their ordering providers that watch for their site loading under someone else's domain, or for checkout sessions that never reach the real payment provider, are well placed to catch these sites early.

item.title: We know 15k websites are infected. how do we tell them? (155 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://scotthelme.co.uk/we-know-15-579-websites-are-infected-how-do-we-tell-them/, See on Hacker News

We've identified 15,579 websites that are currently infected with malicious JavaScript and between them, we conservatively estimate that they receive more than 135 million visits every month.

We know they're infected, and we have the evidence to back that up, but there's a problem: how on Earth do we tell them all?

As our Threat Intelligence capabilities at Report URI have grown, identifying compromised websites has become increasingly efficient. Unfortunately, responsible disclosure hasn't kept pace, and we're now finding infections considerably faster than we could ever hope to notify the affected organisations.

I genuinely don't know how to solve this problem, so I'm asking for help.

What attacks we're finding

At the core of it, we're finding websites that are running JavaScript that they should absolutely not be running! For some examples of how nasty this can be:

  • Credit card skimmers - often known as 'Magecart', they target payment pages and skim full card details to send them to the attacker.
  • ClickFix attacks - designed to trick users into completing a "prove you're human" challenge and instead installing malware on their device.
  • Device exploitation - loading malware to compromise specific versions of iOS and install spyware, like DarkSword or Coruna.
  • Redirects - these can send the visitor anywhere, including fake login pages to phish details, device security 'warnings', scams, and much more.

All of these are bad scenarios for the innocent visitor, and attackers change their payloads depending on their objective.

How these sites are compromised

There are many ways an attacker can get malicious JS onto a site, but here are the main categories that we group the initial vectors into from what we're seeing:

  • Direct compromise - typically a WordPress vulnerability or similar, the site's own JS files are modified to include the malicious JS.
  • Supply chain - a third-party script file that a site loads is infected with malware, and is then loaded on to the site, exposing all visitors.
  • XSS - good old traditional XSS, a vulnerability in the site itself that allows JS to be injected.
  • DeadTag - a threat group we named recently, buying expired domains that sites still load JS from, reviving them, and serving malware.

Unfortunately, there are a lot of different ways that this can go wrong, as we're seeing.

The scale of the problem

Right now, we have 15,579 unique sites that are infected with one of the malicious JS attacks listed above. Those are the sites where there is no doubt in our mind, and the list of sites where we have some suspicion but haven't got to 100% confidence is thousands more. Take September as an example, because we haven't quite finished processing everything from October yet, and this is the tally for new sites that we identified as being infected:

These are the sites that, as of today, are still infected. We remove sites once they clear their own infection as we have no concern about trying to notify them, so there were more than this.

In terms of traffic volumes, it's quite surprising how quickly this adds up. None of the sites in the list are global leaders, but we do have a huge presence of regional leaders. For example, if we look at .fr, .es and .de sites, some of them are really highly ranked sites in those countries, but they barely crack the Top 1 Million globally. Being a top site in France still gets you quite a hefty amount of traffic it turns out. Using various sources of data, and being ultra-conservative with our estimates, our list of currently infected sites is comfortably receiving a combined 135 million visits a month. That's a lot of exposure.

So, what do we do?

We continue to reach out directly to those sites that we identify as particularly high impact and try to notify them, though this is happening on an admittedly small scale. The process of responsible disclosure consumes a lot of resources, use of security.txt is low, and the vast majority of our emails and messages go unanswered. It's simply not possible for us to scale this up.

As these are sites we're crawling and identifying ourselves, we have no contact information like we would for a customer. So, as things currently stand, that's where we are, and I'd like to hear suggestions on what we can do.

If you're from an NCSC/CERT, especially in Europe where we seem to be finding a lot of impacted sites, please reach out to intel@report-uri.com and we'd be happy to provide a list of infected sites in your region. Hopefully you would be able to have more success in notifying the impacted sites than we would.

If you're an organisation and believe having commercial access to our threat intelligence feeds would help you protect your own customers, you can also reach out to intel@report-uri.com for details.

Back to the original problem, though, and it pains me to say it but I don't have a clear idea on how we can try to have more of a positive impact. If you think there's something you can help with, an idea you'd like to put forward, or a suggestion on what we can do with all of this data, please drop by the comments below and I'd be happy to hear from you.

We have intelligence that could help protect millions of website visits, and we need help to turn it into action.

item.title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs (104 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21375, See on Hacker News

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract:Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent 'memory tokens' for a frozen LLM. Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM's input embedding space. Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering. Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108x fewer tokens to represent the source documents. Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent's past turns) increases throughout the trajectory. In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent's tendency to wander between rooms it has already explored, and improves its average success rate from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. Overall, Memorilla aids frozen LLMs in accumulating and using knowledge effectively across long-context interactions and takes a step towards building continually learning AI systems.

item.title: Devvm.dev: One VM for every project (151 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://devvm.dev/, See on Hacker News

Free and open source

One VM for every project

An isolated sandbox with your project’s toolchain, ready for you or a coding agent to start coding.

Install Read the docs

Quick start

1. Go to your project

Open a terminal and cd into any project folder.

2. Run devvm

devvm shows what the new VM gets. Confirm to make it, or customize it.

3. Start your agent

devvm opens a shell in the VM, whose prompt starts with (devvm), so start your agent there.

Claude Code needs your Claude login before its first start, which devvm agent login claude makes from the VM and keeps on your machine (your first VM). The next time you run devvm in the folder, it opens the same VM, and devvm tools adds an agent to a VM you already have.

What’s supported

Toolchains

devvm chooses the toolchains your project’s files call for, and you can choose more when you customize a new VM or name them with --tools (toolchains).

Coding agents

Claude Code, Codex and opencode run in the VM. Choose one when you customize a new VM, or choose them for every new VM in devvm setup (coding agents).

Layers

devvm ships the docker, nix and desktop layers, which you choose when you customize a new VM, and devvm layer new creates your own custom layers you can apply to any of your VMs (layers).

Why use devvm?

  • Developers face attacks every day, such as supply chain attacks, leaked secrets, prompt injections and rogue agents.
  • A sandbox limits the blast radius of an attack to what’s inside it.
  • You know you should run your code and agents in a sandbox, but most tools need configuration and setup that’s hard to get right.
  • devvm ships with sensible defaults so you can start coding in a sandbox with a single command.

Developer ready, zero config

  • The base image comes with optional extras that you choose, such as oh-my-bash, fzf, zoxide (z), tree and tldr.
  • Every VM gets your git name and email, so the commits made in it are authored by you or your agent.
  • Ports forward on their own, so a dev server on :5173 in the VM opens at localhost:5173 on your machine (ports).
  • devvm code opens the VM in VS Code over Remote-SSH (devvm code).

Isolated sandbox

  • The VM mounts your project folder at the same path. Apart from your agents’ settings from devvm’s own store, which it gets read-only, it sees nothing else in your home folder (what a VM can reach).
  • New VMs get the allowlist network tier by default, so they reach only an allowlist of hosts, through a proxy on your machine. You can choose a looser tier, internet or open, or a stricter one, none.
  • On macOS, devvm locks .git’s hooks and config, so the VM can’t change what git runs on your machine (.git protection).
  • With --clone, the VM works on a clone of the repo of its own instead of your folder, so nothing in it can touch your working tree or .git, and its work reaches your repo only when you fetch it.
  • No sandbox closes every gap, so attack vectors lists what’s left open, and staying safe lists the habits that close most of it.

Ready in seconds

  • The first VM builds a base image, and every later VM is a copy of it that starts in seconds (images).
  • devvm builds each version of a toolchain once and shares it read-only, so all VMs use the same copy (shared tools).

Made for coding agents

  • The agent runs in the VM, so an attack on it stays in the sandbox. It gets your settings, skills and MCP servers but never your history (coding agents).
  • On every network tier, their secrets, such as your Claude Code token and your Codex login, stay on your machine, because the VM gets placeholders and devvm’s proxy puts the real ones into its requests on the way out.

Make it yours

  • Your own layers are setup scripts that devvm builds into an image: devvm layer new mailpit starts one, and devvm --layers mailpit makes a VM with it (your own layers).
  • devvm setup --layers gives every new VM the layers you choose, so your shell setup, aliases or dotfiles can go in a layer of your own that each VM gets unless you leave it out (extras of your own).
  • --from starts the base image from a container image instead of Ubuntu’s, such as node:24 or your team’s own (starting from a container image).
  • When the project has a devcontainer.json, devvm sets up its VM from the file’s container image, ports, environment and commands (devcontainer.json).

FAQ

What does it run on?

devvm runs on macOS and on Linux, on arm64 or x86_64. It needs Lima, which runs the VMs with Apple’s Virtualization framework on macOS and QEMU on Linux (backends). Homebrew installs Lima along with devvm, and on Linux, Lima also needs QEMU and access to /dev/kvm. Installing lists every requirement, and known limits lists what Linux hosts lack, such as .git protection.

Does the agent run on my machine?

No. You start the agent in the VM’s shell, so it runs in the VM, and you never install it on your machine. There it sees only what the VM can reach.

Is it free?

Yes. devvm is open source under the MIT license.

Start coding in a sandbox

Install devvm, then run devvm in any project folder.

Install Read the docs
